Planet 10-K: Planet recorded $26.0 million of expense in the fiscal year ended January 31, 2026 for hosting and other services provided by Google, and has minimum purchase commitments for Google hosting services through January 31, 2028 totaling $67,480 thousand.

Planet Q2 FY2027 results: record revenue of $116 million, approximately 58% year-over-year growth; non-GAAP gross margin 59% vs 61% a year earlier; adjusted EBITDA profit $13.9 million. CFO: the outperformance came mainly from satellite services, specifically the handover of the first Pelican for the Swedish Armed Forces (point-in-time revenue).

Planet revenue mix: CFO: defense and intelligence revenue grew more than 90% year-on-year (including satellite services), commercial more than 15%, civil government over 5%; by region approximately 3% in Latin America, over 15% in Asia Pacific, approximately 25% in North America and over 130% in EMEA; point-in-time revenue was 12% of revenue vs 1% a year earlier.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 90%; more than 15%; over 5%; over 130%; 12%

quarterly_data.signal: Planet ACV metrics (exclude satellite services): recurring ACV 98% of end-of-period ACV book of business; approximately 94% annual or multi-year contracts; net dollar retention 109%, 110% with win backs.

Planet backlog: CFO: remaining performance obligations approximately $753 million, up approximately 9% year-over-year (46% within 12 months, 68% within 24 months); backlog including termination-for-convenience contracts approximately $815 million, up approximately 11% (50% within 12 months, 70% within 24 months), implying that by executing on contracts already in backlog Planet could recognize over $400 million in revenue over the next four quarters, not including new business or renewals.

Planet FY2027 guidance (low end raised): revenue $430 million to $441 million (40% to 43% growth); non-GAAP gross margin 55% to 57%; adjusted EBITDA $3 million to $10 million; capex approximately $100 million-$115 million; managing to be adjusted free cash flow positive for the year and aiming for Rule of 40.
quarterly_data.figure: $430 million and $441 million; 40% to 43%; $3 million and $10 million; $100 million-$115 million

quarterly_data.signal: Planet Q3 FY2027 outlook: revenue $101 million to $105 million (approximately 27% year-on-year growth at the midpoint); non-GAAP gross margin 56% to 58%; adjusted EBITDA loss of $6 million to $1 million; capex approximately $30 million-$37 million. CFO: Q2 outperformance partly shifted revenue from Q3 (timing of the satellite handover) without changing the full-year outlook.

Planet capex: CFO: Q2 capex including capitalized software approximately $29 million, just above guidance due to timing of Pelican procurements and AI software development; capex to increase in future quarters to scale manufacturing in San Francisco and Berlin, invest in supply chain resiliency and build next-generation fleets - advance procurements of long-lead items for Pelican and Owl.

Planet satellite services pipeline: CEO: over $4 billion of identified satellite services opportunities, over 25% (about $1 billion) qualified as near-term pipeline (near term meaning quarters, not years), spread across EMEA, APAC and North America and now extending from defense into civil government, though still mainly defense and intelligence deals; Planet delivered a first satellite in orbit within two and four months of contract award for its two most recent satellite services partnerships.

Planet NGA contract (August, after the quarter): new $8 million contract with the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to deploy Planet's Global Monitoring Service (GMS) in support of national defense priorities, with options to expand and extend; CEO: Planet was the only vendor considered; the program grew out of a Defense Innovation Unit pilot in support of INDOPACOM.

Planet German government tender (August): Planet was awarded a tender for dedicated capacity satellite services with options and a maximum possible value of EUR 25 million over five years - Planet's first satellite services deal for a federal civil government agency.

Planet Swedish Armed Forces: the first satellite for the Swedish Armed Forces launched in May, four months after the satellite services contract was signed; Planet completed commissioning and handed over this first sovereign Earth observation satellite in Q2, contributing to the revenue outperformance.

Planet data-center monitoring: Planet signed a six-figure expanded renewal with a hyperscaler AI developer for global monitoring of data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facility construction using Pelican high-resolution data (CEO: Planet's first win with an AI hyperscaler for data center monitoring); CFO: interest in data center monitoring across insurance, energy and financial services.

Planet other deals: a seven-figure one-year agreement with a European defense and intelligence customer for high-resolution global mosaics; a new contract with the Rwanda Space Agency for national high-resolution data and analytics (Planet's first national program of its kind in Africa); a renewal with the New Mexico State Land Office (partnership since 2019, monitoring over 9 million acres); partnerships with FarmQA (AI agronomic tools) and Bragger Technologies (spatial intelligence platform).

Planet maritime domain awareness: CEO: Planet's U.S. Navy partnership alone images 13 million square kilometers of ocean territory; the Navy work was sole-sourced on its second award; Planet is the only company doing a daily scan.

Planet Tanager and SuperDoves: Planet shipped its second Tanager hyperspectral satellite and 18 SuperDoves to the launch site, slated for launch this fall aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission; the second Tanager doubles capacity for methane and CO2 detections for partner Carbon Mapper.

Planet next-generation Pelican tech demo: launched in July with advancements across payload, on-orbit compute and satellite-to-satellite communications, on the path to 30-cm class resolution imagery; not expected to serve customers. CEO: it has RF (not optical) inter-satellite links; optical crosslinks come in later missions, developed in-house together with the main telescope system for an independent supply chain.

Planet Owl: next-generation monitoring satellite upgrading data from 3-m to 1-m class resolution and cutting latency to as little as an hour in key areas, delivering roughly 10 times more data about 10 times faster, with onboard AI detection and satellite-to-satellite communication; Planet is beginning to accelerate the program. CEO: a definite price increase opportunity; customers expect prices to go up.

Planet manufacturing capacity: the new German satellite manufacturing facility is expected to roughly double Planet's manufacturing capacity, with clean room fit-out scheduled for September and building to begin in the facility this year; under a launch partnership announced in July, Isar Aerospace is scheduled to launch a Pelican next year that Planet plans to build in the new German facility.

Planet launch and supply chain: CEO: strong demand for SpaceX rideshare missions; launch prices, about $20,000 a kilogram when Planet started, are now significantly less but have been going up a little; Planet has launched 688 Earth-imaging satellites on 42 rockets of 10 different varieties (SpaceX 16 times, the Indian PSLV seven times) and is investing to secure launch access and diversify; Planet has stockpiled critical components. CFO: advance procurement of longer lead time items is part of the raised capex.

Planet AI: CEO: the AI app (natural-language queries of Planet's 10-year daily archive, model-agnostic) has progressed to open beta; Planet believes it has under 5% market share of the Earth observation market excluding satellite services and that AI is expanding the market to users without geospatial expertise.

Planet long-term targets: CFO: the business can deliver adjusted EBITDA profitability of 25%+ with healthy free cash flow; gross margin target amended to north of 60%, depending on the mix of business.

Planet cash flow: CFO: year to date approximately $68 million net cash from operating activities, free cash flow $21 million and adjusted free cash flow $29 million (excluding non-recurring litigation settlement payments).

Planet U.S. government demand: CEO: the administration is leaning into commercial solutions, with meaningful expansion of commercial-type operational budgets across NGA, NRO and the department; substantial programs are targeted in the government's FY2027, which has not yet passed Congress.

CFO Ashley Johnson: Planet ended the quarter with approximately $865 million of cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, up over 200% year on year on positive free cash flow and proceeds from capital transactions over the last year.

Rocket Lab HASTE contract: a record $266 million contract from the U.S. Space Force for up to 18 suborbital missile defense launches, Rocket Lab's largest launch contract ever and its second multi-year DoD suborbital deal in five months; launches mostly from two new pads at Kodiak, Alaska deployed with the GHOST containerized launch-site technology; CFO: the contract includes funding for infrastructure.

Rocket Lab Flatellite contract: a $397 million contract to build and launch multiple Flatellite spacecraft for the Space Force Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program, to be launched on Neutron; CEO: it is the first Flatellite order, and most of what he could see Rocket Lab doing for itself in the future will be built on the back of a Flatellite platform.

Rocket Lab GEO satellites: two deals totaling more than $160 million to build three geostationary satellites, including a prime contract with the Space Systems Command for two GEO space-domain-awareness satellites carrying the Heimdall payload from acquired GEOST - Rocket Lab's first step into the government GEO satellite market.

Rocket Lab launch bookings: 26 new launches grew the launch backlog to 90+ launches, the highest in its history; 13 launches this year with 100% mission success; NASA signed three Electron launches across two missions next year; iQPS signed another three launches (18 in total); a confidential defense prime booked two HASTE launches in 2027.

Rocket Lab VICTUS HAZE: for the Space Force mission Rocket Lab launched Electron in 16 hours and 42 minutes against a 24-hour requirement, commissioned the spacecraft it built in 38 hours (72 allowed) and tracked, chased and photographed a non-cooperative satellite in less than 59 hours (84 allowed); CEO: the first time the Space Force had ever seen a single prime contractor deliver the rocket, the spacecraft and the orbit operations for the same tactically responsive space mission.

Rocket Lab Iridium acquisition (pending): Iridium brings a constellation of 66 satellites relied upon by more than 2.5 million subscribers and more than $870 million in annual revenue; completion expected in mid-2027 subject to Iridium stockholder and regulatory approvals; CEO: the constellation is good into 2035, growth focus on IoT, direct to device, advanced PNT, defense and aviation / marine safety. Mynaric and Motiv acquisitions closed in the quarter; CEO: likely further tuck-ins, Iridium not a one and done.

Rocket Lab Neutron: production lines up with target delivery of Neutron to the pad in Q4 2026, though the window for an end-of-year launch is narrowing; more than 400 Archimedes hot fires completed and the full engine set for the first launch is in production; stage testing is the last big milestone before flight; planned ramp of 1-3-5 launches.

Rocket Lab Neutron pricing and demand: CFO: Neutron was brought to market at a $50 million-$55 million ASP with no significant discounting for early launches, and sees more upside to ASPs than downside; CEO: zero issues selling full-price Neutrons before the test flight; very limited Neutron supply is being allocated between commercial customers, the government (NSSL) and Rocket Lab's own needs including Iridium.

Rocket Lab launch market: CEO: launch has never been so constrained and options to book a launch, especially after 2029, are extremely limited; the NSSL Lane 1 ceiling tripled from $5.6 billion-$17 billion; competitors' new capacity is largely spoken for by their own internal programs (internets, AI data centers), so the constrained launch market should persist for quite some time.

Rocket Lab space components: CEO: Rocket Lab has scaled its solar business into the largest space-grade solar manufacturer in the world; spacecraft components such as reaction wheels are a moat. CFO: component margins range from the 30s for solar to north of 70 points for some products; satellite platform programs such as SDA Tranche 2 and Tranche 3 (the biggest pieces of backlog) are in the mid-30s; government programs last about four years on a 10/40/40/10 revenue curve.

Rocket Lab orbital data centers: CEO: data centers in space are a real opportunity but he is cautious on their scale; Rocket Lab has released new solar cells specifically targeted at that application and expects to be well positioned if they become real, but is not going to build orbital data centers itself yet.

Rocket Lab Germany: CEO: following the Mynaric acquisition Rocket Lab plans the official establishment of Rocket Lab Germany, seeing a real opportunity to establish a regional hub for constellation-class manufacturing and full-scale spacecraft assembly, integration and test, serving European commercial, civil and defense programs as a domestic provider; Germany has put over $40 billion in place for a satellite missile warning system among other things.

Rocket Lab Mars Telecommunications Orbiter: CEO: Rocket Lab is waiting for NASA to complete its procurement process and feels strongly positioned.

quarterly_data.signal: AST U.S. operators: President: the potential U.S. MNO joint venture does not affect AST's existing agreements with AT&T and Verizon and frees up a third and fourth customer for AST in the United States; CEO: AST plans to keep its current partner contracts as they are and expects to work with all operators in the United States and all major operators in Europe.

AST network deployment: 13 spacecraft in orbit with approximately 20,000 square feet of combined aperture; over 3,000 low-band cellular cells deployed in the U.S., with the remaining cells expected this year to light up the roughly 5,600 cells covering the United States; CFO: BlueBirds 14 to 16 ready to ship shortly, BlueBird 17 through 46 in various stages of production and assembly.

AST manufacturing capacity: 95% vertically integrated manufacturing; over 500,000 square feet of manufacturing and operations space ramping to a target cadence of six fully assembled satellites per month (CEO: currently getting to six per month); plans for an additional 400,000 square feet in Midland, Texas; AST expects its global manufacturing and operations footprint to exceed 1 million square feet, with over 900,000 square feet in the United States, once completed.
quarterly_data.figure: six satellites per month; 400,000 square feet; 1 million square feet

quarterly_data.signal: AST deployment targets: CFO: targeting approximately 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit by early 2027; continuous SpaceMobile service across key markets (U.S., Europe, Japan and others) with approximately 45 to 60 satellites, and a constellation of over 100 BlueBirds for worldwide service. President: consumer-ready capability targeted for later in 2026, commercial service rolling out with as little as 45 satellites in orbit; about 25 satellites give about half the day coverage.

AST launch: President: ten launches booked with two different providers (asked about launches other than Blue Origin), targeting a launch cadence of every month or two on average; Blue Origin is targeting a return this year after the May anomaly, but AST is not betting on that in its numbers; with a mix of launches AST expects to reach its initial 45 satellites in early 2027.

AST technology: CEO: the AST ASIC chip is now in full production and is expected to nearly double the 98.9 megabits per second peak data speed achieved on Block 1 BlueBirds; it supports up to 10 gigahertz of processing bandwidth per satellite (nearly 10x Block 1), with up to an additional 10x user-experience gain expected over time from AI-enabled spectrum management. C-band is already built into the ASIC architecture and a third generation will include L-band MSS, mid-band and C-band; mid-band production starts later this year to begin launching very early in 2027 (current satellites are low-band).

AST spectrum: CEO: satellites can tune approximately 1,150 megahertz of low-band and mid-band spectrum; on the path to approximately 100 megahertz in the U.S. (Ligado spectrum plus MNO partner spectrum) and over 60 megahertz globally; over 3,900 patents and patent-pending claims. President: full U.S. commercial service approvals were delivered earlier this year and multiple countries have authorized use of AST's S-band MSS spectrum outside the United States.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately 1,150 megahertz; approximately 100 megahertz; over 60 megahertz

quarterly_data.signal: AST AI edge compute: CEO: AST is starting to add compute capability on satellites 47 and 48, integrating it into the system later in the year. President: space-based AI edge compute is a target market because AST deploys and controls large structures in space with significant power to orbit at competitive cost; near term AST will stretch from a bent-pipe network to edge computing capabilities.

AST expanded markets: President: new end markets beyond direct-to-device - radar and other government noncommunications, secure communications to low-profile devices, sovereign constellations (J-LEO), federal emergency and backup on the 700-megahertz band (FirstNet with AT&T, Vodafone Ireland), IoT and space-based AI edge compute - could each ultimately become multibillion-dollar annual revenue opportunities.

AST revenue goal: President: nothing has changed in the goal of approaching $1 billion of revenue in the first full year of commercial service; for next year the government opportunity could contribute probably as much as half, plus continued infrastructure revenue and commercial service ramping; on the components of 2027 revenue, gateway is in excess of $100 million as AST continues to grow it; without committing, commercial service revenue recognition should generally begin when commercial service begins next year.
quarterly_data.figure: approaching $1 billion; in excess of $100 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO and Chief Legal Officer Andrew Johnson: on a pro forma basis, including the gross proceeds of its subsequent convertible notes offering, AST's cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash as of June 30, 2026 were over $3.7 billion (CEO Abel Avellan: a balance sheet of more than $3.7 billion).
quarterly_data.figure: pro forma cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash over $3.7 billion (June 30, 2026)

Rocket Lab Mynaric: the Mynaric acquisition closed within Q2 and made an initial contribution to Space Systems revenue at lower gross margins; CFO: the asset had supply chain issues and went through an insolvency process, Rocket Lab had to replenish its supply chain (part of the Q2 cash step-up), volumes rise over the next several quarters, and margins should come in line with the rest of the Space Systems merchant business within a few quarters.
